notes.title: The law about taking a wife back
notes.text: The picture echoes Deuteronomy 24:1-4, which forbids a man to remarry a wife he divorced after she has married someone else. Jeremiah applies it to Israel: after so many lovers, a return looks impossible, yet the LORD still invites her back.

notes.title: aravi
notes.text: The Hebrew word is usually translated "Arab", meaning a people of the desert regions. The picture is someone waiting by the roads, here to attract lovers. "Nomad" is used for the sense, not as a claim about one particular people.

notes.title: A shameless face
notes.text: Hebrew literally says "the forehead of a prostitute woman". The forehead stands for the face a person shows; a hard forehead is one that no longer shows shame.

notes.title: alluf
notes.text: The word can mean a close friend or companion, a guide, or the chief of a clan. A close friend fits the marriage language around it, but it is a judgment call.

notes.title: meshuvah and the word shuv
notes.text: "Apostate" translates meshuvah, "turning away". It belongs to the root shuv, "turn, return". Forms of shuv appear in verses 1, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 14, 19 and 22, and the chapter plays on turning away and turning back.

notes.title: Sound or lightness?
notes.text: The Hebrew consonants can be read as "sound, noise" (the pointing used here) or as "lightness", which would give "because she took her prostitution lightly". Both fit the sense of casual, public unfaithfulness.

notes.title: baalti
notes.text: The verb behind "I am your husband" can also mean "I am your master". The same root gives the name Baal, so the word carries the contrast between the LORD and the Baals of verses 23-24.

notes.title: bosheth
notes.text: Hebrew bosheth means "shame". It is often understood as a stand-in for the name Baal: compare Jeremiah 11:13 and Hosea 9:10, and the name Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel 2:8, who is called Eshbaal in 1 Chronicles 8:33.
